items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: Oh, yes. I knew Jimmy Noon as a kid.

ctx.x: He never did play with Marshall reading bands, did he? No, no, no. You see, he never played sax. He never

played with no bands. I see, yeah. Just in Orleans. Did you know Jimmy Noon down there? Oh, yes. I knew Jimmy Noon as a kid. He took, Jimmy Noon was a hell of a musician. He was high, man. Beautiful, man. He played with Charlie Cook's band. He played with Chicago. He played with Chicago. He threw it sound and oh, he played. He seemed to be very fast.
He wasn't yet. He had a little teenage. Yeah. He took every note. Yeah, he was fast.

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: We copied a lot from Jimmy. Bonnie and I both.

ctx.x: Did you hear much of Jimmy Noon in the old days?

I heard Jimmy Noon when I was a kid, 15 years old. As I told you, he was playing with the Young Olympia Band. In fact, we were taking lessons together with Papa Teo also. Jimmy was a couple of, about four years older than I am. And he was playing a lot of clarinet. And it was Jimmy. Bonnie came after me. Bonnie Begarde studied with Teo also. And Omar Simeon in Chicago, studied with Teo. And Teo was in Chicago. Now, Jimmy was one of the best. When he left New Orleans to join Charlie Cook's band. And when we heard…
acquaintance from him. Would you say he was a real original?

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: Dickie Wells and Jimmy and Dickie, they were two dancers. They were young.

ctx.x: I just wondered who was in those reviews.

Now the names got away from...let's see. Oh yeah, Dickie Wells and Jimmy and Dickie, they were two dancers. They were young. And who else? You had a girl, she came to New York later on. She was a very good singer and dancer, although she used to do a split, and split all across the slope. I've forgotten her name. She was gonna sing a little bit. And who else? Oh. There was a blues singer, a big one like...she was from St. Louis, Missouri. She had a hell of a voice, a big sound like the first blues singer. What's…
When I think of Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith.
